sections.instructions: Answer one of the two extended response questions.
sections.parts: One 12-mark question (AO3).

papers.name: Paper 1
papers.content: Core theme 'Being human' (Section A) and the optional themes (Section B)

sections.name: Section A
sections.instructions: Answer one of the two stimulus-based questions on the core theme.
sections.parts: One task of 25 marks per question
sections.notes: Unseen stimulus (a short text extract or an image) on the core theme 'Being human'. Candidates explore a philosophical issue arising from the stimulus, referring explicitly to the stimulus and to their wider knowledge of the core theme.

sections.name: Section B
sections.instructions: Answer one essay question from the choice of two per optional theme.
sections.parts: One essay of 25 marks
sections.notes: Two essay questions are set for each optional theme, each tied to one required content point of that theme. SL candidates write on the one optional theme they have studied. The question count shown is for a single theme; the paper offers two per optional theme.

papers.name: Paper 1: Engaging with anthropology
papers.content: Part 1 of the syllabus, engaging with anthropology, applied to an unseen ethnographic text of 500-700 words

sections.name: Paper 1
sections.instructions: Answer Questions 1 and 2, then one comparison question (either 3 or 4), then Question 5. All of these are compulsory apart from the choice between 3 and 4.
sections.parts: Q1 description and application of a concept: 4 marks; Q2 analysis and interpretation: 6 marks; Q3 or Q4 comparison: 10 marks; Q5 big anthropological question: 10 marks
sections.notes: The unseen text is 500-700 words. Q3 asks for a comparison based on one of three key concepts with another group or society studied. Q4 asks for a comparison of the text's anthropologist's research approach with that of one other anthropologist. Q5 asks for an argument on one of six big anthropological questions, drawing on the text and wider ethnography. Comparative material must be identified by ethnographic present, historical context, fieldwork location and ethnographer. Paper 1 has both markschemes and assessment criteria.}

papers.name: Paper 2: Engaging with ethnography
papers.content: Part 2 of the syllabus, engaging with ethnography, using areas of inquiry the school has studied

sections.name: Section A
sections.instructions: Answer the one compulsory question. Pick one of three key concepts and one of five real-world issues, and apply them to ethnography from one area of inquiry you have studied.
sections.parts: One question worth 15 marks
sections.notes: The question format is the same every session, but the key concepts and real-world issues change. The area of inquiry is the student's choice and is not named in the question. The real-world issue must be grounded in a contemporary example. Assessed with criteria only, with no markscheme.

sections.name: Section B
sections.instructions: Choose one question from one area of inquiry you have studied. It must be a different area of inquiry from the one used in Section A.
sections.parts: Nine areas of inquiry with two questions each; one question worth 15 marks
sections.notes: Each question refers to a key concept or an inquiry-specific concept. Reusing the Section A area of inquiry caps the Section B essay at 6 marks. The same questions are set for SL and HL, but the assessment criteria differ. Assessed with criteria only.

papers.name: Paper 1: Engaging with anthropology
papers.content: SL material (part 1 engaging with anthropology) plus an HL extension on anthropological ethics

sections.name: Section A
sections.instructions: Answer Questions 1 and 2, then one comparison question (either 3 or 4), then Question 5, all based on the unseen text.
sections.parts: Q1 description and application of a concept: 4 marks; Q2 analysis and interpretation: 6 marks; Q3 or Q4 comparison: 10 marks; Q5 big anthropological question: 10 marks
sections.notes: The unseen text is 500-700 words. At HL, Q3 comparison must include concepts, ethnography and theory. Q4 compares the theoretical and methodological approach of the text's anthropologist with that of one other anthropologist. Q5 asks for an argument on one of six big anthropological questions. Comparative material must be identified by ethnographic present, historical context, fieldwork location and ethnographer. The HL criteria also reward use of anthropological theory.

sections.name: Section B: Anthropological ethics (HL extension)
sections.instructions: Choose one of two stimuli (one written, one visual) and answer the compulsory question on it.
sections.parts: One question worth 10 marks
sections.notes: The question is static and stays the same each session, while the stimuli change. It assesses knowledge and understanding of the ethical issues involved in doing anthropology. Students pick which stimulus to respond to.

papers.name: Paper 2: Engaging with ethnography
papers.content: Part 2 of the syllabus, engaging with ethnography, using areas of inquiry the school has studied (four at HL)

sections.parts: One question worth 15 marks
sections.notes: The question format is the same every session, but the key concepts and real-world issues change. The area of inquiry is the student's choice and is not named in the question. The real-world issue must be grounded in a contemporary example. Assessed with criteria only.

sections.name: Section B
sections.instructions: Answer two questions, each from a different area of inquiry you have studied. Neither may be the area used in Section A.
sections.parts: Nine areas of inquiry with two questions each; each answer is worth 15 marks
sections.notes: Each question refers to a key concept or an inquiry-specific concept. Reusing the Section A area caps that Section B essay. Choosing both questions from the same area caps the second essay. Using one area for all three answers compromises overall achievement. The same questions are set for SL and HL, but the assessment criteria differ. Assessed with criteria only.

papers.name: Paper 1
papers.content: Part 1: Introduction to world religions (all nine religions on offer)

sections.name: Section A
sections.instructions: Choose from Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism. At least one question must come from this section.
sections.parts: (a) 3 marks, (b) 7 marks
sections.notes: Minimum of one answer from this section; the remaining two questions overall may come from any section. Each question gives a short extract (two to four lines) from a text of the religion. Part (a) tests a key idea or concept and may be answered in bullet points. Part (b) tests understanding and application in relation to the text and religion. Part (a) uses question-specific markschemes; part (b) uses question-specific markschemes plus the paper 1 part (b) markbands, with best-fit marking.

sections.name: Section B
sections.instructions: Choose from Judaism, Christianity and Islam. At least one question must come from this section.
sections.parts: (a) 3 marks, (b) 7 marks
sections.notes: Minimum of one answer from this section; the remaining two questions overall may come from any section. Each question gives a short extract (two to four lines) from a text of the religion. Part (a) may be answered in bullet points.

sections.name: Section C
sections.instructions: Choose from Taoism, Jainism and Baha'i Faith. At least one question must come from this section.
sections.parts: (a) 3 marks, (b) 7 marks
sections.notes: Minimum of one answer from this section; the remaining two questions overall may come from any section. Each question gives a short extract (two to four lines) from a text of the religion. Part (a) may be answered in bullet points. Overall the candidate answers five questions in total across the paper for 50 marks; the extra 20 marks come from the two additional questions chosen from any section.

papers.name: Paper 2
papers.content: Part 2: In-depth studies of six world religions; answers relate to the two religions studied in depth

sections.name: Section A
sections.instructions: Choose one essay question from this section (Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism). Two questions are specific to each religion and one is open-ended. Two questions are answered overall, each from a different section.
sections.parts: Each essay is worth 20 marks
sections.notes: Six specific questions (two per religion) plus one open-ended question answerable in relation to any of the three religions. Open-ended answers need specific, contextualized examples referring to denomination, culture and geography; broad generalizations earn no credit. Candidates draw on primary and/or secondary sources. Marked with question-specific markschemes and the paper 2 markbands, best-fit.

sections.name: Section B
sections.instructions: Choose one essay question from this section (Judaism, Christianity, Islam). Two questions are specific to each religion and one is open-ended. Two questions are answered overall, each from a different section.
sections.parts: Each essay is worth 20 marks
sections.notes: Six specific questions (two per religion) plus one open-ended question answerable in relation to any of the three religions. Open-ended answers need specific, contextualized examples referring to denomination, culture and geography; broad generalizations earn no credit. Candidates draw on primary and/or secondary sources. Marked with question-specific markschemes and the paper 2 markbands, best-fit.

papers.name: Paper 1: Guided literary analysis
papers.content: Two previously unseen literary passages from different literary forms; not tied to works studied in class

sections.notes: Each passage comes from a different literary form and has a guiding question on a technical or formal element. Answering the guiding question is optional, but the analysis must have a focus; students may propose their own point of entry.

sections.parts: Criterion A 5 marks, B1 5 marks, B2 5 marks, C 5 marks, D 5 marks.
sections.notes: Written without access to the studied works. Detailed reference is expected but quotations are not required. Same paper and questions for SL and HL.

papers.name: Paper 1: Guided literary analysis
papers.content: Two previously unseen literary passages from different literary forms; not tied to works studied in class

papers.name: Paper 1: Productive skills—writing
papers.content: Draws on the five themes (identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organization, sharing the planet); factual topic knowledge is not tested.

sections.name: Paper 1
sections.instructions: Choose one of three writing tasks, each based on a different theme, and write 250–400 words in a text type chosen from those listed in the examination instructions.
sections.parts: One response of 250–400 words; marked out of 30 across Criterion A Language (12), Criterion B Message (12) and Criterion C Conceptual understanding (6).
sections.notes: Tasks vary in audience, context and purpose. Three assessment criteria with markbands, plus detailed marking notes for examiners. Dictionaries and reference materials are not allowed. A response ignoring context, purpose and audience may score 0 for criteria B and C even with a high Criterion A mark.

papers.name: Paper 2: Receptive skills—listening and reading
papers.content: Draws on all five themes; tests understanding of the passages, not factual content of a topic. All passages and answers are in the target language.

sections.name: Listening comprehension
sections.instructions: Answer comprehension exercises on three audio passages, in the target language. Time allowed: 45 minutes.
sections.parts: Three audio passages; 25 marks in total.
sections.notes: Requires audio playback. Passages may show linguistic variation and regional accents. Dictionaries are not allowed. Marked with a markscheme.

sections.name: Reading comprehension

papers.name: Paper 1: Productive skills—writing
papers.content: Draws on the five themes; factual topic knowledge is not tested. Tasks demand more complex language and higher-order thinking (analysis, evaluation, synthesis, interpretation) than at SL.

sections.name: Paper 1
sections.instructions: Choose one of three writing tasks, each based on a different theme, and write 450–600 words in a text type chosen from those listed in the examination instructions.
sections.parts: One response of 450–600 words; marked out of 30 across Criterion A Language (12), Criterion B Message (12) and Criterion C Conceptual understanding (6).
sections.notes: Tasks vary in audience, context and purpose. Three assessment criteria with markbands, plus detailed marking notes. A response ignoring context, purpose and audience may score 0 for criteria B and C.

papers.name: Paper 1
papers.content: Unseen extract in Latin or Classical Greek; no prescribed texts needed

sections.name: Paper 1
sections.instructions: Choose one of two options (one prose extract, one verse extract) and answer all questions on it. A Latin or Classical Greek dictionary is allowed.
sections.parts: Short answer questions on comprehension and language knowledge, no evidence needed 10 marks; one short answer question citing evidence from the extract 4 marks; translation of about one-third of the extract 16 marks
sections.notes: Latin extract about 130 words, Classical Greek about 150 words, with citation, introduction in the response language, and summaries or glosses where suitable. Short answers use item-specific markschemes. Translation is marked with markbands (6 marks for holistic quality) plus an item-specific markscheme (10 marks for precision across 10 words or phrases).

papers.name: Paper 2
papers.content: Prescribed core text chosen by the school, plus supplementary reading

sections.name: Paper 2
sections.instructions: Choose the one option on the core text you studied. Answer the short answer questions on its extract, then respond to one of the two prompts. No dictionary allowed.
sections.parts: Short answer questions on the extract 20 marks; extended response to one of two prompts 12 marks
sections.notes: Each option has an extract of about 30 lines (170 words) from a different core text. Short answer tasks may include explaining context, analysing literary features, translating short passages and scanning poetry (Latin: hexameters and elegiacs; Greek: hexameters and iambic trimeters). The extended response uses evidence from the core text and supplementary reading. Short answers use an item-specific markscheme and the extended response uses assessment criteria (knowledge and evidence, analysis and evaluation, 6 marks each). Extracts and prompts are shared with HL Paper 2.

papers.name: Paper 1
papers.content: Two unseen extracts in Latin or Classical Greek, one prose and one verse; the first extract is the same as on the SL paper

sections.name: Paper 1
sections.instructions: Choose one of two options, each with two unseen extracts, and answer all questions on that option. A Latin or Classical Greek dictionary is allowed.
sections.parts: First (longer) extract: short answer questions 10 marks, short answer citing evidence 4 marks, translation 16 marks. Second (shorter) extract: short answer using evidence from both extracts 4 marks, guided analysis of the second extract 6 marks
sections.notes: The first extract and its questions match the SL paper in that session. The second extract is in the opposite literary form, with a short summary in the response language, and is about 65 words in Latin or 70 in Greek. In one option the prose extract is longer, in the other the verse extract. Translation is marked with markbands (6) plus an item-specific precision markscheme (10). The 4-mark question uses an item-specific markscheme and the guided analysis uses markbands.

sections.name: Paper 2

sections.parts: Short answer questions on the extract 20 marks; extended response to one of two prompts 12 marks
sections.notes: Each option has an extract of about 30 lines (170 words) from a different core text. papers.name: Paper 1
papers.content: One focused study from each option, chosen by the examiners for each exam session; students must learn both studies in each option but only one is examined

sections.name: Paper 1
sections.instructions: Answer all three questions, which are the same every year, using sources A, B and C. All questions ask how the sources can be used to address a single inquiry question stated at the start of the paper.
sections.parts: Question 1: 6 marks; Question 2: 6 marks; Question 3: 12 marks
sections.notes: Static question format: only the inquiry question and the three sources change. Sources are a mix of primary and secondary and may be written, pictorial, diagrammatic or multimodal. Q1 explains how content of sources A and B can be used; Q2 analyses how the context of source C affects its use; Q3 examines how the perspectives in all sources can be used. Uses generic markbands plus a paper-specific markscheme.

sections.name: Section B

sections.notes: Two questions on each of the four thematic studies (8 in total); the student answers one question, both parts. Part (b) essays must use examples from at least two regions. No prescribed essay format. Generic markbands plus paper-specific markscheme.
